flagged.title: Identity & Heritage
flagged.reason: The video completely misattributes the poems, claiming Grace Nichols wrote 'Name Journeys' (written by Raman Mundair) and Sumia Jaama wrote 'Like an Heiress' (written by Grace Nichols), which would severely penalise students in a GCSE literature exam.

mark_affecting.video_says: Let's look at the title of her poem: Name Journeys. In Nichols's invisible backpack, names themselves are what travel...
mark_affecting.lesson_says: Raman Mundair — 'Name Journeys' (Mundair wrote 'Name Journeys', whereas Grace Nichols wrote 'Like an Heiress').

mark_affecting.video_says: We're looking at British Somali poet Sumia Jaama... Her poem is called Like an Heiress...
mark_affecting.lesson_says: Grace Nichols — 'Like an Heiress' (Grace Nichols wrote 'Like an Heiress', not Sumia Jaama).

flagged.title: Migration & Displacement
flagged.reason: The video misattributes the poem 'A Century Later' to Arundhathi Subramaniam instead of Imtiaz Dharker and completely misrepresents its subject matter and themes.

mark_affecting.video_says: Subramaniam and the Unreachable Home... Arundhathi Subramaniam and her poem A Century Later
mark_affecting.lesson_says: "A Century Later" is by Imtiaz Dharker, not Arundhathi Subramaniam, and explores a girl claiming education despite violence (inspired by Malala Yousafzai), rather than a migrant returning to an unreachable homeland.

mark_affecting.video_says: surrounded by white passengers who actively refuse to acknowledge his presence
mark_affecting.lesson_says: The poem focuses on a white Quaker woman who "startled me" by speaking to him first and talking warmly of racial brotherhood, representing connection across racial lines alongside casual racism.

flagged.title: Memory & Time
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly attributes the anthology poem 'The Jewellery Maker' to Patience Agbabi rather than Louisa Adjoa Parker and asserts it is an extended metaphor when the lesson explicitly states it is not.

mark_affecting.video_says: see how the brilliant British-Nigerian poet, Patience Agbabi, acts as the artisan... The Jewellery Maker
mark_affecting.lesson_says: Louisa Adjoa Parker — 'The Jewellery Maker'. Parker, a writer of English and Ghanaian heritage, draws a close portrait of a real craftsman.

mark_affecting.video_says: Agbabi uses the figure of a jewellery maker as an extended metaphor for the craft of memory and storytelling
mark_affecting.lesson_says: The poem is not an extended metaphor but a study in small detail

flagged.title: Power, Politics & Protest
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly attributes the anthology poem 'pot' and its biographical context to Imtiaz Dharker instead of shamshad khan, which would penalise students in a GCSE exam.

mark_affecting.video_says: Imtiaz Dharker draws from her own life navigating multiple cultures. In her poem Pot, she takes this everyday, simple domestic object...
mark_affecting.lesson_says: shamshad khan — 'pot'. khan is a second-generation British Asian poet from Manchester. The poem was commissioned for the city’s museum and is written as a conversation with a Nigerian pot in its collection.

flagged.title: Form, Structure & Language
flagged.reason: The video attributes anthology poems and techniques to the wrong poets (Fiona Benson instead of Liz Berry for 'Homing', Patience Agbabi, Imtiaz Dharker instead of shamshad khan for the pot, and Grace Nichols instead of Raman Mundair for the sound of names), which would lose marks for text knowledge in an exam.

mark_affecting.quote: Think of Fiona Benson's Homing... Benson uses visual and tactile imagery... Patience Agbabi's entire poem acts as one giant extended metaphor where jewellery equals memory, and Imtiaz Dharker uses a simple pot... Grace Nichols uses the rich musical sounds of different names
